main_message: Gibraltar's repeated sieges and its disputed isthmus, runway and frontier explain why Spain and Britain still argue over it, and the last 'siege' is now about jobs and paperwork.

claims_doubted.quote: Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
claims_doubted.why: Counts vary by author (some list 14, others 15 or 12, depending on what counts as a siege vs a blockade). 'Historians on both sides' is vague, and Sayer, García Sanz and the museum are cited as one bundle for a number that is a convention, not a fact. Say that the count is conventional.

claims_doubted.quote: Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
claims_doubted.why: Opening claim stated flatly, yet the closing section says the treaty is only provisionally applied pending a European Parliament vote. 'No routine checks' needs the same hedge up front, and 'no routine checks' is not the same as 'no checks'.

claims_doubted.quote: To walk in from Spain, you cross an airport runway.
claims_doubted.why: True for pedestrians, but no source is given in this chapter and the 'only about 150 metres' detail later suggests the arrangement is being changed. Check it is still true at publication.

claims_doubted.quote: Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
claims_doubted.why: Too compressed. England was by then Great Britain only from 1707, and the Allies' candidate was the Archduke Charles; 'Madrid's king' hides that Philip V was the legitimate heir by Charles II's will. Neutral, but it flattens the dynastic dispute that made the capture a pretext.

claims_doubted.quote: The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
claims_doubted.why: No counter named. Commonly cited figure is around 15,000 shot over about two days, but it is a British-derived figure and not attributed.

claims_doubted.quote: Spain besieged it twice more: from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and in 1727. Neither siege took it.
claims_doubted.why: 'Twice more' is wrong or confusing: the 1704-05 siege is the Franco-Spanish siege under Villadarias/Tessé, which sits inside the 1704 chapter, and the 1727 siege followed Utrecht (1713). Chronology jumps from 1713 back to 1704 and the 'twice more' skips the failed 1704-05 relief by Leake and Byng.

claims_doubted.quote: Britain said in 2015 that it does.
claims_doubted.why: Vague. Britain has long asserted title to the isthmus on the basis of prescription/long occupation; 2015 is just one statement. 'Said in 2015' needs a named document, otherwise it implies a new position.

claims_doubted.quote: By Spanish accounts, almost all left, and the largest group settled a league north-east, at San Roque.
claims_doubted.why: Disputed point: British historians (e.g. Jackson) note some civilians stayed and that the exodus was largely voluntary and complete by a few months. 'Almost all' is Spanish framing stated without a count. Also San Roque is north-west, not north-east, of the Rock, so check the compass point.

claims_doubted.quote: On the twenty-first of June 1779, Madrid cut Gibraltar off from Spain.
claims_doubted.why: Spain declared war 16 June 1779 and the frontier closure followed; 21 June is conventional but say the source.

claims_doubted.quote: Scurvy spread, until a Danish ship of lemons was brought in, garrison diaries record.
claims_doubted.why: Anecdote leans on diaries with no named diarist; also the relief of scurvy is usually tied to the 1780 arrival of Rodney's fleet and to supplies from Morocco, so a single ship is an oversimplification.

claims_doubted.quote: On the twelfth of April 1781, the second relief convoy dropped anchor, and Spain's batteries opened fire on the town.
claims_doubted.why: Causal ordering is unclear. Spanish bombardment of the town began on 12 April as a direct response to the convoy, but the sentence reads as simultaneous coincidence and omits that the bombardment destroyed most of the town. Also the next lines cut off the human cost.

claims_doubted.quote: By British tallies, the two sides fired over four hundred and sixty thousand rounds.
claims_doubted.why: Tally source is 'British' but undefined; cannot be checked and stands alone with no context on how many were Spanish.

claims_doubted.quote: The garrison turned to heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire.
claims_doubted.why: Overstated: red-hot shot ignited wood and powder but did not set everything alight, and heated-shot use began in 1782 (Eliott had furnaces built after the Spanish floating battery threat). 'Whatever they hit' is dramatic.

claims_doubted.quote: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish.
claims_doubted.why: Montero and Fernández Duro quote 50, but this is a combined Franco-Spanish fleet, and the on-screen quote 'a joy to see' is cherry-picked rhetoric from a nationalist-era source.

claims_doubted.quote: A French account says he'd asked to test them against red-hot shot first. It was refused.
claims_doubted.why: This is d'Arçon's own self-justifying defence, presented in the 1785 inquiry. Treating it as neutral French evidence without saying the inventor was the source overstates it. The batteries were also claimed to be fireproof, which the script never states.

claims_doubted.quote: By the next afternoon, all ten batteries were lost.
claims_doubted.why: Batteries were burned or abandoned by the early hours of 14 September after the Spanish/French themselves set them alight. 'Lost' is vague on whether destroyed by garrison fire, by Spanish crews or by the British boats' Curtis intervention.

claims_doubted.quote: the British rescued three hundred and fifty-seven.
claims_doubted.why: Number is from the British return, which includes Captain Curtis's gunboats. Whether that is the full count of rescued is not stated, and the on-screen numbers (>2,000 lost, 185 hit before fires, 357 rescued) do not obviously reconcile.

claims_doubted.quote: Garrison: 16 killed — its own return
claims_doubted.why: Widely quoted figure for 13 September; a very lopsided ratio that will sound like propaganda unless it is clearly labelled as the garrison's own count and cross-checked.

claims_doubted.quote: By early July, Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
claims_doubted.why: Specific and plausibly from Drinkwater or Connolly, but the dates are muddled: the Upper Galleries digging began in 1782 and the 'Notch' was reported around May-July 1782; but 'all summer' before the September attack is fine. Needs a source on screen.

claims_doubted.quote: The blockade never forced a surrender.
claims_doubted.why: True, but it omits that the garrison came close to starvation before the 1781 relief and that the 1783 peace, not the defence alone, ended the siege. Reads as a British victory narrative.

claims_doubted.quote: The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and sixty-nine dead.
claims_doubted.why: 333 + 536 = 869, which is consistent with the on-screen card. However, it is called 'at least' and then the card says scurvy deaths for 1779-80 are not included, so 869 is clearly not the full garrison figure and should be stated as a minimum from the Drinkwater return.

claims_doubted.quote: In 1810, with Napoleon's armies heading for the Strait, Spain and Britain were allies. With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
claims_doubted.why: Date uncertainty is acknowledged on screen (Montero 1811), but the narration states 1810 flatly. 'With Spain's consent' rests on a single Spanish source and is the foundation of British claims to the isthmus works, so state who gave consent (the Cadiz Regency).

claims_doubted.quote: In 1870, it became La Línea de la Concepción.
claims_doubted.why: Date of the formal municipal creation is 1870 (some sources 1870 for independent municipality status). Fine, but unsourced here.

claims_doubted.quote: In 1908, Britain told Spain, "as an act of courtesy," that it would fence the edge of the neutral ground. The fence went up in 1909; Spain does not recognise it as a border.
claims_doubted.why: Presents Spain's position on the fence but never states the British legal position (that the area was occupied de facto since the 1800s and acquiesced to). Asymmetric.

claims_doubted.quote: That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fait accompli, like the Rock itself.
claims_doubted.why: Unattributed in the narration and the on-screen source covers March 1939 only. Needs the November document cited.

claims_doubted.quote: Gibraltar counts about fifty-five kilometres of tunnels from every era, more than its roads above ground.
claims_doubted.why: 'Counts' is good, but 'more than its roads' is a bold comparison with no source; Gibraltar's tunnel network is often cited as ~34 miles (about 55 km), the road network is roughly 50+ km depending on definition. Verify.

claims_doubted.quote: By 1942, the invasion of North Africa is run from inside the Rock.
claims_doubted.why: Overstated. Eisenhower's HQ for Operation Torch was in a tunnel at Gibraltar, but the planning and command were Anglo-American and spread across London and Washington. 'Run from inside the Rock' is a flourish.

claims_doubted.quote: June 1940: Spain turns "non-belligerent" and occupies Tangier.
claims_doubted.why: Spain declared non-belligerence on 12 June 1940 and occupied Tangier on 14 June. Correct, but it is said without noting that Britain tolerated the Tangier occupation, and without noting Spain stayed out of the war.

claims_doubted.quote: at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway
claims_doubted.why: Attributed to Gibraltar's official record, but the number is high-end and the 'at least' is odd; sources cited elsewhere usually give a few hundred aircraft staged. Verify and state who counted.

claims_doubted.quote: Britain counted some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers cut off.
claims_doubted.why: Reasonable, but 'Britain counted' is vague (Gibraltar government? UK government?).

claims_doubted.quote: The gate fully reopened in 1985.
claims_doubted.why: Pedestrian access reopened in 1982 and full reopening was in February 1985 after Brussels. OK, but it skips the 1982 partial reopening.

claims_doubted.quote: In October 2025, people living in Spain held more than four in ten of Gibraltar's jobs.
claims_doubted.why: 'More than four in ten' conflicts with the later numbers (14,000 jobs out of about 38,000 residents' economy is not the same base). No stated denominator; and the 15,000 daily crossers vs 14,000 jobs held by people in Spain are both used without reconciling.

claims_doubted.quote: In 2024, La Línea's unemployment was twenty-eight point six percent: the highest of a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities.
claims_doubted.why: Source and measure unnamed (which survey, registered vs survey-based). The ranking among 113 cities needs a named dataset.

claims_doubted.quote: Gibraltar's government puts output per resident at about eighty-five thousand pounds.
claims_doubted.why: Presented as a 'twist' and then dismantled with 'Our read', which is the narrator's own inference, not sourced. Check the figure and the year.

claims_doubted.quote: Our read: part of the work behind that number is done from the other side.
claims_doubted.why: Editorial inference with no source; it also tilts toward the Spanish-side-benefit argument and ignores that Gibraltar's output includes online gaming, finance and shipping whose staff are not all cross-border.

claims_doubted.quote: Today, four in ten of the Rock's jobs are held by people who live beyond it.
claims_doubted.why: Rounding: earlier text says 'more than four in ten' and elsewhere 14,000 jobs; make the three figures agree and name the base.

claims_doubted.quote: The last siege ended in 1783. The argument didn't.
claims_doubted.why: Good line, but 'the last siege' contradicts the 1779-83 being treated as the fourteenth, and glosses over the 1969-85 closure, which many Gibraltarians call a 'siege' (a loaded term the video never addresses).

one_sided.quote: Inside, Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count. He refused to surrender.
one_sided.why: Gives only the Spanish garrison count first and frames Salinas as defiant; the British figure of up to 500 only comes later and is qualified as 'counting armed townsmen', which looks like a rebuttal. The narrative of a handful of men overwhelmed by 15,000 rounds is emotive.

one_sided.quote: Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown
one_sided.why: 'Rival' and quoting 'Charles the Third' in scare quotes frames the capture as an act on behalf of a pretender and delegitimises the British role, without noting that Gibraltar was initially taken in the Archduke's name and that many Spaniards backed him (Catalonia, Aragon).

one_sided.quote: But "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
one_sided.why: Quoted from Article X without the following sentence on the Spanish right of first refusal, or the British interpretation. Cherry-picks the restrictive clauses.

one_sided.quote: Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain said in 2015 that it does.
one_sided.why: Spain's position is stated as a long-standing claim; Britain's is reduced to a single date in 2015, which suggests it is a recent assertion rather than a position held since the 18th century.

A one-sided casualty ratio presented as a card, with the attacker figure resting on British and Montero estimates. Without a Spanish/French count for their dead, the contrast reads as a British triumph.

one_sided.quote: The governor, General Eliott, could hold the walls. The food had to come by sea.
one_sided.why: Heroic framing of Eliott; omits criticism of his harsh discipline and the fact that the garrison's survival depended on the Royal Navy and, notably, on supplies from Morocco, which is not mentioned.
Implicitly blames the Spanish bombardment for civilian suffering with no counter-sentence on British actions, such as the looting that followed.

one_sided.quote: Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchants' stores. A British officer blamed "resentment and intoxication."
one_sided.why: Includes an unflattering British episode but with no balancing example from the Spanish lines, where desertion, disease and ill-discipline were also documented.

one_sided.quote: A French account says he'd asked to test them against red-hot shot first. It was refused.
one_sided.why: Implies the Franco-Spanish defeat was due to a refused test, an excuse favoured in Spanish and French tradition; it quietly downplays the garrison's gunnery and Curtis's flank attack.

one_sided.quote: In July they blasted a hole for air. A Spanish historian wrote it was big enough for a cannon.
one_sided.why: Uses a Spanish historian to validate a British engineering legend, which is neat, but the 'hole for air' vs 'cannon embrasure' contradiction is brushed aside and the British version is allowed to win.
Closes the siege chapter on a flat triumphant note, right after listing Spanish losses at 'six thousand besiegers'.

one_sided.quote: A Spanish historian describes Britain advancing into the neutral zone step by step.
one_sided.why: Only the Spanish view of the creeping frontier is given; there is no British account of how the area came to be occupied or the legal basis for it.

one_sided.quote: The fence went up in 1909; Spain does not recognise it as a border.
one_sided.why: Ends on Spain's non-recognition with no statement of the British/Gibraltar position.
Repeats Spanish wording as the headline for the airfield without an equivalent British justification (e.g. the 1938-39 defence needs and long-standing occupation).

one_sided.quote: no complaint over the airstrip is on record.
one_sided.why: A Spanish scholar's finding that Spain did not protest during the war is useful, but it is slanted toward the British legal argument of acquiescence and is presented without noting Spain's wartime difficulties or the reasons for silence.

one_sided.quote: In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
one_sided.why: Gives only Spain as the actor and omits the trigger (Gibraltar's 1969 Constitution and Franco's response) and the subsequent UN decolonisation context.

Tone: the twist is that Gibraltar's wealth leans on Spanish workers while La Línea suffers, which is framed as a reproach to Gibraltar and ignores the tax, regulatory and structural reasons for La Línea's unemployment.

one_sided.quote: Our read: part of the work behind that number is done from the other side.
one_sided.why: Implies Gibraltar's prosperity is partly borrowed from Spain; no counter-view is offered.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
casualty_counter_missing.why: No source or counter for the round count.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: British accounts put the defenders at up to five hundred, counting armed townsmen.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Does not name which British account, and 'up to' is a ceiling, not a count.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: about fourteen thousand Spanish troops faced the Rock.
casualty_counter_missing.why: 'By the British count' is given, but no named document or date; the Spanish figure is absent.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: By British tallies, the two sides fired over four hundred and sixty thousand rounds.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Which British tally? No author, no split between the sides, and the rounds are not distinguished (shot, shell, musketry).

casualty_counter_missing.quote: By September 1782, the garrison counted about seven and a half thousand men.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Garrison counted by whom, and does it include sailors, civilians, Hanoverians and the Royal Artillery?

casualty_counter_missing.quote: At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, the attackers' guns, some four hundred, opened fire together.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Gun count 'some four hundred' is vague, and it is unclear whether it is Spanish ordnance or the combined total of ships, batteries and land guns.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: By British and Spanish counts, over two thousand attackers were lost, prisoners included
casualty_counter_missing.why: 'Lost' lumps killed, drowned, wounded and captured. The on-screen card cites 'British estimate & Montero', which is two sources but no breakdown; the 185 'hit by gunfire' number is from a French account and its counter is not explained.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: the British rescued three hundred and fifty-seven.
casualty_counter_missing.why: 'British return' on screen but narration does not say it. Unclear whether this includes the wounded.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: the Spanish historian Montero put the losses near two thousand defenders and six thousand besiegers.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Montero is a 19th-century historian and his figures are an estimate; no explanation of what he counted from, and 'from all causes' makes it non-comparable to the garrison return.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and sixty-nine dead.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Source is on screen (Drinkwater), but the narration says 'the garrison's own records'. Neither the dates nor the categories (killed, died of wounds, sickness) are spoken.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Attributed to 'Gibraltar's official record' without naming the document or date.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: Britain counted some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers cut off.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Which British body counted, and what date?

casualty_counter_missing.quote: The UK government puts the daily crossers at about fifteen thousand.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Source named, but the year, and whether it includes tourists and residents, are not.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: the highest of a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities.
casualty_counter_missing.why: No dataset or statistical agency named.

hard_to_follow.quote: So why, today, is the fight over it about paperwork and payrolls?
hard_to_follow.why: Opening question introduces 'paperwork and payrolls' before the audience knows the frontier regime or jobs data, so it is abstract when heard once.

hard_to_follow.quote: Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
hard_to_follow.why: Dense: five parties and a succession dispute in one breath, with no names. A first-time listener will lose who is who.

hard_to_follow.quote: On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered.
hard_to_follow.why: The calendar discrepancy is only on screen (24 July old style); someone listening will be confused by two dates in the later sentence about English histories.

hard_to_follow.quote: Spain besieged it twice more: from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and in 1727.
hard_to_follow.why: Timeline loops back to 1704 after 1713; the listener cannot follow the order, and 'twice more' is hard to count.

hard_to_follow.quote: The treaty never mentions the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain said in 2015 that it does.
hard_to_follow.why: 'It does' is ambiguous: it does what? A listener cannot tell if 'it' is Britain, the treaty or the isthmus.

hard_to_follow.quote: By the next afternoon, all ten batteries were lost.
hard_to_follow.why: Hard to picture the sequence of 13-14 September when the numbers are delivered over a fast montage.

hard_to_follow.quote: By British and Spanish counts, over two thousand attackers were lost, prisoners included; the British rescued three hundred and fifty-seven.
hard_to_follow.why: Several figures in one sentence (2,000, 357) plus on-screen 185 and 16. Heard once, the arithmetic does not hold together.

hard_to_follow.quote: From all causes, the Spanish historian Montero put the losses near two thousand defenders and six thousand besiegers. The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and sixty-nine dead.
hard_to_follow.why: Two incompatible totals (2,000 vs 869) back to back with different categories; the listener will not know which to trust or how they differ.

hard_to_follow.quote: This was the gap between them: a strip of neutral ground between two towns.
hard_to_follow.why: Visual-dependent sentence with no content for an audio-only listener.

hard_to_follow.quote: Remember this street in La Línea. We'll come back to it.
hard_to_follow.why: Relies on a visual the listener may not remember eight minutes later.

hard_to_follow.quote: Why build an airfield on disputed ground? In March 1939, Spain protested that the works stood on "a usurped portion" of its territory.
hard_to_follow.why: Chronology confusing: 1934 airstrip, March 1939 protest, November 1939, 1941 runway, then back to 1940 and 1942. Dates jump.

hard_to_follow.quote: That spreads output over the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs.
hard_to_follow.why: Hard to parse by ear: per-capita GDP logic, a population figure and a job count in two clauses.

hard_to_follow.quote: It says it changes neither side's position on sovereignty. In July, Gibraltar's government said the old fence was coming down, with a new one a few metres behind; only about a hundred and fifty metres, where walkers cross, stays open.
hard_to_follow.why: 'It' refers back to the treaty two sentences earlier; the fence details and the 150 metres are tangled.

hard_to_follow.quote: As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is applied provisionally, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
hard_to_follow.why: Legalistic and date-heavy for an audio ending.

boring_or_slow.why: Treaty detail, then a sudden skip through two sieges, then a 1730 wall. It is a stretch of administrative history with little for a viewer to feel.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: By British tallies, the two sides fired over four hundred and sixty thousand rounds.
boring_or_slow.why: A run of numbers (rounds, garrison strength, ship counts) between the key dramatic beats; the middle drags before the batteries arrive.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: After that, the edge kept moving.
boring_or_slow.why: Abstract frontier legal history with no character or event; the pace drops and the 'Subscribe' prompt in the middle of a fence-and-racecourse list breaks the mood.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: Gibraltar counts about fifty-five kilometres of tunnels
boring_or_slow.why: The tunnel-and-map section is fascinating in principle but is told as a list; the silent shot and the 1943 map description add little narration value.
Statistics (jobs share, crossers, unemployment, output per resident) delivered one after another without a human story; the ending turns into a briefing.

top3_fixes: Give every casualty and strength figure a named counter in the spoken line (e.g. 'Drinkwater's return', 'Montero's estimate') and split killed, wounded, captured and sick; reconcile or explicitly flag the 2,000 / 357 / 185 / 16 / 869 / 6,000 numbers so a listener can tell they are not comparable.

Rebalance the sovereignty and frontier passages: for every Spanish position quoted (Article X 'for ever' limits, 'usurped portion', non-recognition of the fence, 'step by step' advance) add the British or Gibraltarian position in the same breath, and remove loaded tags such as 'Here's the twist' and 'Our read' unless sourced; also soften the opening 'no routine checks' to match the provisional-application caveat at the end.

Fix the chronology and listening load: tidy the 'Spain besieged it twice more' sequence (1704-05, 1727) so it follows 1713 in order, cut the number-heavy stretches in the middle and final chapters to the two or three figures that matter, and replace sentences that only work on screen ('Remember this street', 'This was the gap between them') with spoken anchors.
_prompt:
You are a British fact-checker for a history magazine with a background in 18th-century military history. You flag any claim that sounds wrong, overstated or unsourced, any number without a stated counter, and any wording that tilts toward the Spanish side or sneers at Britain.

Below is the complete narration script of a documentary YouTube video titled "Why Gibraltar Was Besieged 14 Times" (about 11 minutes, English narration, animated maps and 3D reconstructions). Lines in [On screen: ...] are text shown on screen at that moment; [silent shot] means picture and music only. Read all of it as yourself and answer honestly. Do not be polite; you have no stake in who made it.

Check especially: (a) factual claims that seem wrong, overstated or missing a source; (b) sentences that favour one side (British or Spanish) by wording, emphasis or omission; (c) any casualty or loss number that does not say who counted it; (d) sentences that are hard to understand when heard once; (e) stretches where you would get bored or leave.

Return ONLY this JSON (no other text). In every "quote", copy the exact words from the script (a short exact phrase is fine):
{"main_message": "<one sentence>",
 "would_keep_watching_after_30s": true|false, "hook_1to10": n, "trust_1to10": n, "balance_1to10": n, "overall_1to10": n,
 "claims_doubted": [{"chapter": "<chapter title>", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "one_sided": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "favours": "British|Spanish", "why": "..."}],
 "casualty_counter_missing": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "hard_to_follow": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "boring_or_slow": [{"chapter": "...", "from_quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "top3_fixes": ["<concrete>", "<concrete>", "<concrete>"]}

=== SCRIPT ===
## Midnight at the Gate
Midnight at the Gibraltar frontier. To walk in from Spain, you cross an airport runway.
Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
The Rock sits at the western gate of the Mediterranean.
Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
This is why everyone fought over it, told from both sides' records.
[On screen: "A history explainer · every date sourced · British and Spanish records side by side · Facts as of 18 Oct 2026"]
[On screen: number card "14 sieges · 1309–1783" — "Sayer 1862 · García Sanz 2022 · Gibraltar National Museum"]
In 1782, ten floating batteries came to break it.
In 1941, a runway was laid across the only road to Spain.
So why, today, is the fight over it about paperwork and payrolls?

## 1704: A Rock Changes Hands
Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
That summer, their fleet sailed into the Bay of Gibraltar.
Its commanders, Admiral George Rooke and Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt, came in the name of the rival claimant, "Charles the Third."
This plan, printed in 1705, shows the prize: a walled town that historians on both sides would call the key of the Mediterranean.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «la preciosa llave del Mediterráneo» — "the precious key of the Mediterranean" · Sayer, 1862: "the key of the Mediterranean"]
Inside, Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count. He refused to surrender. The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «con cien hombres de guarnición … no había artilleros que las sirvieran» — "a garrison of a hundred men … there were no gunners to serve them"]
On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered.
[On screen: "4 August 1704 · English histories: 24 July 1704 (old calendar)"]
British accounts put the defenders at up to five hundred, counting armed townsmen.
Townspeople could stay if they swore loyalty to "Charles the Third." By Spanish accounts, almost all left, and the largest group settled a league north-east, at San Roque.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se habia acampado en las haciendas cercanas á la ermita de San Roque» — "had camped on the farms near the hermitage of San Roque"]
In 1713, the Treaty of Utrecht made it permanent: the town, castle and port went to the British Crown, "for ever." But "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
The treaty never mentions the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain said in 2015 that it does.
Spain besieged it twice more: from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and in 1727. Neither siege took it.
So in 1730, Philip the Fifth ordered a stone line across the isthmus, out of gun range, to cut Gibraltar off by land. The town behind it is still called La Línea: "the line."
[On screen: Gómez Nadal (Almoraima), on Philip V's order of 8 Oct 1730: «bloquear definitivamente la correspondencia y paso a la plaza por tierra» — "to block, once and for all, all contact with and passage to the town by land"]

## The Great Siege
Half a century later came a different question: can you starve a rock? On the twenty-first of June 1779, Madrid cut Gibraltar off from Spain.
Spain had joined France in its war with Britain. By October, by the British count, about fourteen thousand Spanish troops faced the Rock.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Carlos III declaró la guerra á Inglaterra y se unió á Francia» — "Charles III declared war on England and joined France"]
At sea, from mid-July, a Spanish squadron sealed the port. Based at Algeciras, its boats were there to cut off the food reaching the Rock from Africa.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «encaminado principalmente á privar a la plaza de los viveres que le llegaban de las costas de África» — "aimed above all at depriving the town of the food that reached it from the coasts of Africa"]
By January 1780, thistles, dandelions and wild leeks were daily food for many; an egg cost sixpence.
The governor, General Eliott, could hold the walls. The food had to come by sea.
To break the blockade, Britain sent three relief fleets: 1780, 1781, 1782.
Scurvy spread, until a Danish ship of lemons was brought in, garrison diaries record.
On the twelfth of April 1781, the second relief convoy dropped anchor, and Spain's batteries opened fire on the town. The townspeople fled south.
Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchants' stores. A British officer blamed "resentment and intoxication."
By British tallies, the two sides fired over four hundred and sixty thousand rounds.
By September 1782, the garrison counted about seven and a half thousand men.
The garrison turned to heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire. On the eighth of September, they used them in earnest against the Spanish works.
Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets gathered in the bay: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish. The Duc de Crillon led the siege.
[On screen: Fernández Duro, Armada española (1901): «alegrando la vista los 50 navios que se juntaron en Algeciras» — "the 50 ships of the line that gathered at Algeciras, a joy to see"]
Their answer to red-hot shot: ten floating batteries, designed by the French engineer d'Arçon. A French account says he'd asked to test them against red-hot shot first. It was refused.
[On screen: Conseil de guerre privé (1785): «l'expérience que l'inventeur avoit demandée … à l'épreuve des boulets rouges» — "the test the inventor had asked for … against red-hot shot"]
The thirteenth of September 1782. That morning, the batteries moved into position, and the garrison opened fire on them. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, the attackers' guns, some four hundred, opened fire together. By the next afternoon, all ten batteries were lost.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «á las diez y veinte y cinco minutos de la mañana … rompieron á un tiempo el fuego» — "at twenty-five past ten in the morning … opened fire all at once"]
By British and Spanish counts, over two thousand attackers were lost, prisoners included; the British rescued three hundred and fifty-seven.
[On screen: number card: "> 2,000 lost, prisoners included — British estimate & Montero (Spain)" · "185 hit by gunfire before the fires — French account, 1785" · "357 rescued — British return" · "Garrison: 16 killed — its own return" {S069} {S070} {S071}]
Before the attack, all summer, the garrison had been digging through the north face. By early July, Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
In July they blasted a hole for air. A Spanish historian wrote it was big enough for a cannon.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se formó un boquete tan grande … que pareció bien colocar en el un cañón» — "an opening was made so large … that it seemed right to place a cannon in it"]
The blockade never forced a surrender. In February 1783, word came of a preliminary peace, and on the fifth, the last shot was fired.
From all causes, the Spanish historian Montero put the losses near two thousand defenders and six thousand besiegers. The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and sixty-nine dead. Gibraltar stayed British.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Los últimos sufrieron una pérdida de cerca de dos mil hombres. La nuestra se aproximó á seis mil por todas causas» — "The latter [the besieged] suffered a loss of nearly two thousand men. Ours came close to six thousand, from all causes" · number card: "Garrison return (Drinkwater): 333 killed or died of wounds · 536 died of sickness (scurvy deaths 1779–80 not included)"]

## The Neutral Ground
Which leaves a question the treaty never answered: where does the Rock end? Between the walls and the Spanish line lay a strip of sand: the neutral ground.
In 1810, with Napoleon's armies heading for the Strait, Spain and Britain were allies. With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
[On screen: Gómez de Avellaneda: «con autorización española, fueran destruidos por los ingleses» — "with Spanish authorisation, they were destroyed by the British" · "Montero gives 1811"]
After that, the edge kept moving. A Spanish historian describes Britain advancing into the neutral zone step by step.
[On screen: García Sanz, 2022: «el progresivo avance de la frontera sobre la zona neutral» — "the gradual advance of the frontier over the neutral zone"]
On the Spanish side, a town grew up behind the old line. In 1870, it became La Línea de la Concepción.
Remember this street in La Línea. We'll come back to it.
This was the gap between them: a strip of neutral ground between two towns.
In 1908, Britain told Spain, "as an act of courtesy," that it would fence the edge of the neutral ground. The fence went up in 1909; Spain does not recognise it as a border.
[On screen: García Sanz, 2022: «"como acto de cortesía"» — "as an act of courtesy"]
Behind the fence: a garrison camp, gardens, rifle ranges, a racecourse.
And from 1934, a grass airstrip was built there. Subscribe if you'd like the next place in this series.

## A Runway on the Isthmus
Why build an airfield on disputed ground? In March 1939, Spain protested that the works stood on "a usurped portion" of its territory.
That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fait accompli, like the Rock itself. Late in 1939, Britain began a hard runway; in 1941, it was laid across the only road to Spain.
[On screen: Spanish government to its London ambassador, 4 Mar 1939 (Marquina Barrio, 1981): «una porción usurpada del territorio nacional» — "a usurped portion of the national territory"]
Then Britain pushed it out into the bay, with stone blasted from the north face and rubble from new tunnels.
Inside the Rock, those tunnels held a road about a mile long, a hospital and a power station, dug by British and Canadian tunnellers.
Gibraltar counts about fifty-five kilometres of tunnels from every era, more than its roads above ground.
This 1943 US Army map shows the town house by house, and the runway reaching into the bay.
June 1940: Spain turns "non-belligerent" and occupies Tangier. Gibraltar sends its women and children away. By 1942, the invasion of North Africa is run from inside the Rock.
[silent shot]
For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found, Spain protested what it called breaches of Spanish waters; no complaint over the airstrip is on record.
[On screen: Marquina Barrio, 1981: «no queda constancia de reclamaciones por el uso de la pista» — "there is no record of complaints over the use of the strip"]
On the night of the seventh of November 1942, by Gibraltar's official record, at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway. The invasion fleets, from Britain and the United States, came through the Strait.

## The Gate
After the war, the argument returned to the gate. In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
Britain counted some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers cut off. The gate fully reopened in 1985.
The same square, today. In October 2025, people living in Spain held more than four in ten of Gibraltar's jobs.
The UK government puts the daily crossers at about fifteen thousand. People on foot still cross the runway.
And on the other side of the gate.
Remember this street? In 2024, La Línea's unemployment was twenty-eight point six percent: the highest of a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities.
Here's the twist. Gibraltar's government puts output per resident at about eighty-five thousand pounds.
That spreads output over the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs. Our read: part of the work behind that number is done from the other side.
In July 2026, Britain and the EU signed a treaty; the next day, routine checks here ended.
It says it changes neither side's position on sovereignty. In July, Gibraltar's government said the old fence was coming down, with a new one a few metres behind; only about a hundred and fifty metres, where walkers cross, stays open.
As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is applied provisionally, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
So why did everyone fight over this place? Where it sits, and the sea that could feed it. A wall in 1704. A line in 1730. A fence in 1909. A runway in 1941.
[silent shot]
In 1730, Spain built a line to cut the Rock off by land. Today, four in ten of the Rock's jobs are held by people who live beyond it. The last siege ended in 1783. The argument didn't. Next in Contested Places: London, 1666.
